html:
The Bar Kokhba revolt was the last great Jewish rising against the Roman Empire, fought in Judaea from 132 to 136 CE. Its defeat emptied much of Judaea of its Jewish population and pushed the centre of Jewish life elsewhere.

Sixty years earlier the Romans had destroyed the Second Temple in Jerusalem. Around 130 CE the emperor Hadrian decided to rebuild the ruined city as a Roman colony, Aelia Capitolina, with a temple to Jupiter. That plan, and perhaps a ban on circumcision, set off the revolt.

Its leader was Simon bar Kosiba, called Bar Kokhba, "son of the star". Some, including the great teacher Rabbi Akiva, hailed him as the Messiah. The rebels set up an independent state for over three years and struck their own coins. Letters from Bar Kokhba himself were found in desert caves in the 1950s and 1960s.

Rome sent some of its best generals and many legions. They wore the rebels down village by village, and in 135 or 136 CE took their last fortress, Betar.

The results were terrible:

  • Ancient writers record huge numbers of dead, and many survivors were sold as slaves.
  • Jews were barred from Jerusalem, except to mourn on one day a year.
  • Rome renamed the province Syria Palaestina.

Jewish life moved to Galilee and to Babylonia. There rabbis gathered the oral law into the Mishnah around 200 CE, the foundation of rabbinic Judaism, which held together a people now scattered in the diaspora.
sum: The Bar Kokhba revolt was the last great Jewish rising against the Roman Empire, fought in Judaea from 132 to 136 CE. Its defeat emptied much of Judaea of its Jewish population and pushed the centre of Jewish life elsewhere.
